newsitem.title: FRANCE: De Silguy says no-one can predict euro fx rate.
newsitem.headline: De Silguy says no-one can predict euro fx rate.

text.p: No-one can predict today whether the euro will be strong or weak, European Commissioner for Economic and Monetary Affairs Yves-Thibault de Silguy said in an interview published on Wednesday.
"They would be clever men who could predict the level of the euro against the dollar," he said in an interview with financial daily Les Echos.
His comments were the latest in a growing debate in France over the appropriate exchange rate for the euro against the dollar.
French officials have said repeatedly that the dollar is undervalued against European currencies.
President Jacques Chirac said in Tokyo on Tuesday that Europe needed a powerful currency which would allow it "to resist the aberrant fluctuations in the dollar".
De Silguy said he was certain the euro would be a stable currency, but that there were contradictory influences in determining whether it would be strong or weak.
Europe, in the single currency zone, was likely to attract investment from non-European central banks and fund managers drawn to the new, big and liquid market.
But European companies in turn would also want to diversify their holdings in dollars and yen.

"Moreover, central banks in the euro zone could unload a part of the very significant holdings which they have in dollars. Which would push up the euro. On the other hand, they could be tempted to dispose in advance of their reserves in European currencies which will lose their usefulness from 1999," he said.
The big change, he said, would be in the level of openness in the euro zone -- given that the ratio of imports to gross domestic product would fall to 10 percent from around 30 percent.
"In other words, the risk of imported inflation will be less, and this will not be without importance in the conduct of monetary policy by the European central bank," he said.

Europe was unlikely to follow a policy of benign neglect on the euro's exchange rate, given the probable importance of the new currency for countries with close ties to the European Union -- in eastern Europe, the Mediterranean region and Africa.
He described as strange a call by some French politicians for a commitment that the euro should not be overvalued against the dollar.
"No-one can honestly say whether the euro will be strong or weak. Moreover the value of currencies is not established by decree.

"It is determined by financial markets which take account of a series of factors. The euro-dollar parity will depend on the monetary policy conducted on both sides of the Atlantic, wage developments, budgetary policies and of course, political events," he said.
